By Thomas

Jobs awaiting parts and jobs ready for work used to appear on separate paper sheets at Fenwick Instrument Repairs, which services brass and woodwind instruments. In January 2026 the workshop team began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule, choosing Benchline after checking that it could distinguish the two statuses. This account draws on the workshop's trial summary and an email interview with its manager, Priya Vale.

## Fenwick set the rules and Benchline configured them

The workshop defined the statuses and decided who would update them. Benchline configured those choices and trained four staff in one online session. Collection arrangements stayed on the telephone, where the team continued to discuss them with customers.

Asked by Benchline's case writer what the team had to settle before the schedule was useful, Vale answered: ‘We had to agree what ready for work meant. A part being in the building did not always mean that it had reached the right bench.’

# Shared schedule showed Fenwick which jobs awaited parts

For six weeks, Fenwick Instrument Repairs trialled a shared Benchline schedule for its bench work. Workshop manager Priya Vale explains what the team had to settle first, what the trial did and did not establish, and what Vale would do differently.

By Thomas

Jobs awaiting parts and jobs ready for work used to appear on separate paper sheets at Fenwick Instrument Repairs, which services brass and woodwind instruments. In January 2026 the workshop team began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule, choosing Benchline after checking that it could distinguish the two statuses. This account draws on the workshop's trial summary and an email interview with its manager, Priya Vale.

## Fenwick set the rules and Benchline configured them

The workshop defined the statuses and decided who would update them. Benchline configured those choices and trained four staff in one online session. Collection arrangements stayed on the telephone, where the team continued to discuss them with customers.

Asked by Benchline's case writer what the team had to settle before the schedule was useful, Vale answered: ‘We had to agree what ready for work meant. A part being in the building did not always mean that it had reached the right bench.’

## Summary records visibility but leaves speed unmeasured

The workshop's trial summary, dated 23 February 2026, lists 38 jobs entered in the schedule. It says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts. It does not measure repair duration, revenue or customer satisfaction, so it records the team's reported experience rather than any measured change in repair speed.

Vale approved continued use for new jobs but postponed adding the backlog until the team had reviewed its status definitions.

## Vale looks back on the choice

Vale was also asked whether the same choice would be made again, and what would change. ‘I would use it again for new jobs,’ Vale replied. ‘I would allow another week to check the status names before adding the backlog.’

A workshop weighing a shared schedule of its own can start with the question Fenwick's team had to answer: what each status means on its benches, and who updates it.
EOF

arguments.content:
# Claim check: Fenwick Instrument Repairs case (draft.md against source.md)

Scope: every factual and attributed claim in the draft, including the title, standfirst, headings and closing line, compared with the material. The source and the draft are both in English, so no crossing between languages and no translated quotations are involved. The byline "By Thomas" comes from the invocation and is not assessed.

## Claim accounting

### Title
- Draft: "Fenwick reports staff could see jobs awaiting parts"
- Source: "The workshop's trial summary ... It says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts."
- Difference: "Fenwick reports" is the workshop's own summary, so the assertion stays with the right party. "jobs awaiting parts" and "instruments waiting for parts" are two names for the same status. The source itself names that status "jobs awaiting parts". The tense and certainty are the same ("says" / "reports"). No case separates the two statements. Supported.

### Standfirst
- Draft: "Fenwick Instrument Repairs put a Benchline bench schedule on trial."
- Source: "the workshop team began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule ... The team chose Benchline". Supported.
- Draft: "Here is what the team had to agree first"
- Source: Question: "What did the team have to settle before the schedule was useful?" Vale: "We had to agree what ready for work meant."
- Difference (time): the source says the agreement was needed "before the schedule was useful". It does not say when the agreement happened relative to the start of the trial. The standfirst's "first" comes straight after "put ... on trial", so it naturally reads as "before the trial began". Case: the team started the trial, found in its second week that "ready for work" was ambiguous and agreed a definition then. The source statement still holds in that case. The standfirst's reading does not. No supplied statement rules this case out. See Finding 1.
- Draft: "what the trial established and what manager Priya Vale would change"
- Source: "workshop manager Priya Vale"; "what would you change?" / "I would allow another week to check the status names before adding the backlog." Supported.

### Paragraph 1
- Draft: "Jobs awaiting parts and jobs ready for work used to sit on separate paper sheets"
- Source: "Previously, jobs awaiting parts and jobs ready for work appeared on separate paper sheets." Same meaning. Supported.
- Draft: "Fenwick Instrument Repairs, which services brass and woodwind instruments"
- Source: "Fenwick Instrument Repairs services brass and woodwind instruments." Supported.
- Draft: "In January 2026 the team began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule"
- Source: "In January 2026 the workshop team began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule." Supported.
- Draft: "choosing Benchline after checking that it could tell the two statuses apart"
- Source: "The team chose Benchline after checking that it could distinguish these statuses." The draft's "it" refers to Benchline, as in the source (third person, singular, no natural gender). "tell ... apart" has the same meaning as "distinguish". The participle does not date the choice more precisely than the source does. Supported.
- Draft: "The workshop's trial summary and manager Priya Vale's emailed answers record how it went."
- Source: "The workshop's trial summary, dated 23 February 2026"; "email interview on 2 March 2026 between Benchline's case writer and workshop manager Priya Vale"; "The summary and interview establish the team's reported experience". "emailed answers" matches the source. "record how it went" does not go beyond "reported experience". "it" refers to the trial. Supported.

### Heading: "Fenwick set the rules and Benchline configured them"
- Source: "The workshop defined the statuses and decided who would update them. Benchline configured those choices". "rules" covers exactly the status definitions and the update responsibilities. "them" is plural and refers to those choices. Supported.

### Paragraph 2
- Draft: "Benchline trained four staff in one online session."
- Source: "Benchline ... trained four staff in one online session." Supported.
- Draft: "It configured the statuses the workshop had defined, and the workshop decided who would update them."
- Source: "The workshop defined the statuses and decided who would update them. Benchline configured those choices". "It" refers to Benchline. The draft says Benchline configured the statuses, which is part of "those choices". It does not deny that Benchline also configured the update responsibilities. The past perfect "had defined" matches the source's order, since Benchline configured choices the workshop had already made. Supported.
- Draft: "Collection arrangements were still discussed with customers by telephone."
- Source: "The team continued to use telephone calls to discuss collection arrangements with customers." "still" has the same meaning as "continued". The passive voice drops "the team" but gives no other agent. Neither statement says telephone was the only channel. Supported.

### Quotation 1
- Draft: "Asked by Benchline's case writer what had to be settled before the schedule was useful, Vale wrote: ‘We had to agree what ready for work meant. A part being in the building did not always mean that it had reached the right bench.’"
- Source: "Question: “What did the team have to settle before the schedule was useful?” Vale: “We had to agree what ready for work meant. A part being in the building did not always mean that it had reached the right bench.”"
- The question is paraphrased with its meaning and its "before the schedule was useful" qualifier intact. "wrote" matches an email interview ("The interview took place by email."). The quotation is verbatim, and its pronouns ("We", "it") are Vale's own. The quote is approved for publication ("Publication of the extract was approved by Vale."). Supported.

### Heading: "Summary covers what staff could see, not repair speed"
- Source: "It says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts. It does not measure repair duration"; "not a measured improvement in repair speed". Supported.

### Paragraph 3
- Draft: "The workshop's trial summary, dated 23 February 2026, records 38 jobs entered in the schedule. It says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts, but it does not measure repair duration, revenue or customer satisfaction."
- Source: the same wording, sentence for sentence. The "but" joins two of the source's statements without adding any claim. Supported.

### Paragraph 4
- Draft: "Vale approved continued use for new jobs but postponed adding the backlog until the team had reviewed its status definitions."
- Source: "The manager approved continued use for new jobs but postponed adding the backlog until the team had reviewed its status definitions."
- Difference (referent): the draft names Vale, while the source says "The manager". The material names only one workshop manager ("workshop manager Priya Vale"), and the brief refers to "its manager" in the singular, so the context settles the referent. "its" refers to the team, as in the source. No natural gender is given. Supported.

### Heading: "Vale looks back on the trial"
- This heading introduces Vale's emailed answer about the trial. Supported.

### Quotation 2
- Draft: "Asked whether the choice would be the same again, and what would change, Vale replied: ‘I would use it again for new jobs. I would allow another week to check the status names before adding the backlog.’"
- Source: "Question: “Would you make the same choice again, and what would you change?” Vale: “I would use it again for new jobs. I would allow another week to check the status names before adding the backlog.”"
- Difference (subject of the question): the paraphrase replaces "you" with an impersonal wording ("the choice would be the same", "what would change"). This is a report of the question, not a quotation. Vale's first-person answer shows the question was put to her own choice, and no concrete case makes the reported question true while the actual question is false, or the reverse. The quotation is verbatim. "replied" suits an email answer. Supported.

### Closing line
- Draft: "A workshop weighing a shared schedule can start with the question Fenwick's team had to answer: what ready for work means on its benches."
- Factual part: "the question Fenwick's team had to answer" rests on Vale's "We had to agree what ready for work meant", which answers a question about "the team". Supported.
- The advice to other workshops is the author's own reflection resting on supported material. It does not attribute a recommendation to Fenwick or Vale, so it does not conflict with "not ... a recommendation for every workshop". The modal "can" presents the advice as optional. Here "its" refers to the hypothetical workshop, and no natural gender is given. No finding. Editorial note, not a defect: the brief supplies no call to action, so whether to keep a closing piece of general advice is the publisher's decision.

### Pronouns: person, number and natural gender
- Draft pronouns outside quotations: "it" (Benchline, the trial), "It" (Benchline, the summary), "them" (the statuses), "its" (the team, a hypothetical workshop). All are third person, and each has the same number as its referent. None states a natural gender.
- The draft never uses a gendered pronoun for Vale, and the source gives none.
- Pronouns inside quotations ("We", "I", "it") are Vale's own and are verbatim.
- No finding.

## Findings (source support)

### Finding 1: standfirst "had to agree first" adds a timing the material does not give
- Draft passage: "Here is what the team had to agree first, what the trial established and what manager Priya Vale would change."
- Source passage: Question: "What did the team have to settle before the schedule was useful?" Vale: "We had to agree what ready for work meant."
- What changes: the time. The source ties the agreement to the point when the schedule became useful. It does not say whether the agreement came before or during the trial. Directly after "put ... on trial", "first" reads as "before the trial began".
- Case: the team agreed the definition of "ready for work" in the middle of the trial, once the ambiguity came to light. The source statement holds in that case and the standfirst's reading fails. No supplied statement rules the case out. The body (paragraph 2) keeps the correct qualifier, but the standfirst drops it.
- Smallest supported repair: "Here is what the team had to agree before the schedule was useful, what the trial established and what manager Priya Vale would change."

## Translation findings
None. Source and draft are both English, and no quotation is translated.

## Completion status
Complete. Every claim in the draft has been accounted for. One source-support finding is unresolved (Finding 1, standfirst timing). There are no translation findings. One editorial note is not a defect: the closing line gives general advice to other workshops, which the brief does not supply.

# Claim check: Fenwick Instrument Repairs case (en_GB)

Source: work/source.md (Brief + Material). Draft: scratch/write-LGEW4K/draft.md.
Source and draft are both English. No quotation is translated, so this check has no translation findings. The byline "By Thomas" comes from the invocation and is not checked.

## A. Claim accounting

| # | Draft passage | Source passage (verbatim) | Difference / assessment |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Title: "Shared schedule showed Fenwick which jobs awaited parts" | "The workshop's trial summary … It says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts." / "The summary and interview establish the team's reported experience" | The title drops the attribution ("It says"), so the summary's report becomes a fact in the publisher's voice. The active verb "showed" makes the schedule the cause of the staff's view. The source says staff "could see", but no passage says the schedule is how they saw it. "jobs" replaces "instruments". **Finding F1.** |
| 2 | Standfirst: "Fenwick Instrument Repairs tested a Benchline bench schedule for six weeks." | "In January 2026 the workshop team began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule." / "The workshop's trial summary, dated 23 February 2026" | The source says a six-week trial *began* and does not say it ran its full length. The draft says the testing lasted six weeks. **Finding F2.** "Benchline bench schedule" is supported ("The team chose Benchline"). |
| 3 | Standfirst: "Here is what the team had to agree first, what the trial established and what manager Priya Vale would change." | Question: "What did the team have to settle before the schedule was useful?" Vale: "We had to agree what ready for work meant." / "I would allow another week…" / Brief: "Show … what the trial established" | This is a signpost that previews supported content. "first" means "before the schedule was useful", so the time frame matches. "trial established" uses the brief's own wording, and the body keeps the qualifier that the summary did not measure speed. Supported. |
| 4 | "Jobs awaiting parts and jobs ready for work used to sit on separate paper sheets at Fenwick Instrument Repairs, which services brass and woodwind instruments." | "Previously, jobs awaiting parts and jobs ready for work appeared on separate paper sheets." / "Fenwick Instrument Repairs services brass and woodwind instruments." | "used to" matches "Previously". Supported. |
| 5 | "In January 2026 the team began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule, choosing Benchline after checking that it could tell the two statuses apart." | "In January 2026 the workshop team began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule. … The team chose Benchline after checking that it could distinguish these statuses." | "tell … apart" means "distinguish". "the two statuses" means "these statuses" (awaiting parts, ready for work). Pronoun "it": third person, singular, non-personal (neuter), referring to Benchline, the same as in the source. The participle clause does not put the choice after the trial began. Supported. |
| 6 | "The workshop's trial summary and manager Priya Vale's emailed answers record how it went." | "The workshop's trial summary, dated 23 February 2026…" / "email interview on 2 March 2026 between Benchline's case writer and workshop manager Priya Vale" | Both sources and the medium are named correctly. "it": singular, non-personal, referring to the trial. Supported. |
| 7 | Heading: "Fenwick set the rules and Benchline configured them" | "The workshop defined the statuses and decided who would update them. Benchline configured those choices" | "rules" sums up the status definitions and the updating responsibilities. "them": third person plural, non-personal, the same as "those choices". Supported. |
| 8 | "Benchline trained four staff in one online session." | "Benchline … trained four staff in one online session." | Identical. Supported. |
| 9 | "It configured the statuses the workshop had defined, and the workshop decided who would update them." | "The workshop defined the statuses and decided who would update them. Benchline configured those choices" | "It": singular, non-personal, referring to Benchline. "them": plural, non-personal, referring to the statuses; the source has the same pronoun and referent. The draft names only the statuses as what Benchline configured. It does not deny that Benchline also configured the updating choices, so it narrows the claim without contradicting it. The pluperfect "had defined" is supported, because Benchline configured choices the workshop had already made. Supported. |
| 10 | "Collection arrangements were still discussed with customers by telephone." | "The team continued to use telephone calls to discuss collection arrangements with customers." | "still" matches "continued". The passive drops the agent ("the team"), but no other agent is implied. The draft does not say telephone was the only channel. Supported. |
| 11 | "Asked by Benchline's case writer what had to be settled before the schedule was useful, Vale wrote: 'We had to agree what ready for work meant. A part being in the building did not always mean that it had reached the right bench.'" | Question: "What did the team have to settle before the schedule was useful?" Vale: "We had to agree what ready for work meant. A part being in the building did not always mean that it had reached the right bench." / "email interview … between Benchline's case writer and workshop manager Priya Vale" | The question is paraphrased faithfully; dropping "the team" changes nothing because the answer says "We". "wrote" is correct, since the interview was by email. The quotation is verbatim, with British single quotation marks. The quoted "We" is first person plural (Vale and the team) and "it" refers to the part; both are Vale's own. No gendered pronoun is used for Vale anywhere in the draft. Supported. |
| 12 | Heading: "Summary records visibility but leaves speed unmeasured" | "It says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts. It does not measure repair duration" / "not a measured improvement in repair speed" | The heading attributes the claim to the summary. "visibility" is shorthand for the staff's view of instruments waiting for parts, and the body spells this out straight away. "speed" corresponds to "repair duration" / "repair speed". Supported. |
| 13 | "The workshop's trial summary, dated 23 February 2026, lists 38 jobs entered in the schedule." | "The workshop's trial summary, dated 23 February 2026, records 38 jobs entered in the schedule." | "records" becomes "lists". Read naturally, "lists 38 jobs" says the summary itemises the jobs. The source supports only a record of 38 entered jobs, which could be a bare total. **Finding F3 (minor).** |
| 14 | "It says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts, but it does not measure repair duration, revenue or customer satisfaction." | "It says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts. It does not measure repair duration, revenue or customer satisfaction." | Verbatim apart from the conjunction. "It": singular, non-personal, referring to the summary. Supported. |
| 15 | "Vale approved continued use for new jobs but postponed adding the backlog until the team had reviewed its status definitions." | "The manager approved continued use for new jobs but postponed adding the backlog until the team had reviewed its status definitions." | "The manager" is Vale ("workshop manager Priya Vale"). "its": singular, non-personal, referring to the team, as in the source. Supported. |
| 16 | Heading: "Vale looks back on the trial" | The interview is dated 2 March 2026, after the trial summary. | Supported. |
| 17 | "Asked whether the choice would be the same again, and what would change, Vale replied: 'I would use it again for new jobs. I would allow another week to check the status names before adding the backlog.'" | Question: "Would you make the same choice again, and what would you change?" Vale: "I would use it again for new jobs. I would allow another week to check the status names before adding the backlog." | The impersonal paraphrase keeps the content of the question. "replied" is neutral. The quotation is verbatim, and its hedge and scope ("for new jobs") are kept. The quoted "I" (first person singular) is Vale and "it" is the schedule/Benchline, both in the source. Supported. |
| 18 | "A workshop weighing a shared schedule can start with the question Fenwick's team had to answer: what ready for work means on its benches." | Vale: "We had to agree what ready for work meant. A part being in the building did not always mean that it had reached the right bench." / "not … a recommendation for every workshop" | This is the author's (publisher's) suggestion, built on supported material. The modal "can" offers a starting point and does not recommend the schedule to every workshop. The factual element, that Fenwick's team had to settle what ready for work meant, is supported. "its": singular, non-personal, referring to "a workshop". It is not a finding. |

## B. Findings (source support)

### F1: The title states the summary's report as fact and adds causation
- Draft: "Shared schedule showed Fenwick which jobs awaited parts"
- Source: "It says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts." / "The summary and interview establish the team's reported experience, not a measured improvement…"
- What differs:
  1. Whose assertion it is. The source attributes the statement to the trial summary; the title gives it in the publisher's own voice.
  2. Cause. "showed" makes the schedule the means by which staff saw the status. The source records only that staff "could see".
- Concrete case, compatible with the material: staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts, and the summary says so, but they saw it partly by checking the parts area or the old sheets rather than through the schedule. The summary's statement holds and the title fails. No supplied statement rules this case out.
- The body (heading and line 17) keeps the attribution; only the title loses it.
- Smallest supported repair: "Fenwick's trial summary: staff could see which instruments awaited parts". Alternatively: "Trial summary says Fenwick staff could see which instruments awaited parts".

### F2: "tested … for six weeks" asserts that the full trial period ran
- Draft (standfirst): "Fenwick Instrument Repairs tested a Benchline bench schedule for six weeks."
- Source: "In January 2026 the workshop team began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule." / "The workshop's trial summary, dated 23 February 2026"
- What differs: time and completion. The source gives the trial's planned length and says that it began. It does not say that testing lasted six weeks.
- Concrete case, compatible with the material: the trial began on 20 January 2026 and the summary was written on 23 February, about five weeks in, and the manager then approved continued use. The draft's claim that the schedule was tested for six weeks then fails. No supplied statement gives the start date or says the six weeks were completed.
- Smallest supported repair: "Fenwick Instrument Repairs began a six-week trial of a Benchline bench schedule in January 2026." Line 7 already uses the supported wording.

### F3 (minor): "lists 38 jobs" in place of "records 38 jobs"
- Draft: "The workshop's trial summary, dated 23 February 2026, lists 38 jobs entered in the schedule."
- Source: "…records 38 jobs entered in the schedule."
- What differs: how the summary presents the information. "lists" reads as an itemised list of jobs, while "records" fits a bare count.
- Concrete case, compatible with the material: the summary contains only the line "38 jobs entered". The source statement holds, but "lists 38 jobs" in its itemising sense fails. Nothing supplied describes the summary's format.
- Smallest supported repair: replace "lists" with "records".

## C. Translation findings

None. Source and target language are both English, and both quotations are reproduced verbatim.

## D. Pronoun accounting (summary)

- Non-personal "it"/"its"/"them" (lines 7, 11, 17, 19, 25): the referents are Benchline, the trial, the statuses, the summary, the team and "a workshop". Person, number and non-personal gender match the source or follow from it.
- Quoted "We" and "I" (lines 13, 23): these are Vale's own words, taken verbatim.
- Vale: no third-person pronoun is used, so the draft makes no natural-gender assertion about her. The source makes none either.

## Completion status

The check is complete. All 18 claim units were compared with the source. There are 3 unresolved source-support findings: F1 (title attribution and causation), F2 (six-week duration stated as completed) and F3 (minor: "lists" for "records"). There are no translation findings.
